summary: Defines a Blocks Extensible Exchange Protocol (BEEP) profile that lets a BEEP peer act as an application-layer proxy. Authorized users can use it to reach services through a firewall. It is on the standards track as a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: A firewall is a locked gate. This lets a trusted helper at the gate carry your message through for you, as long as you are on the approved guest list.

subtitle: A BEEP profile that lets a peer act as an application-layer proxy, so authorized users can reach services through a firewall.

tldr.problem: Machines on one side of a firewall sometimes need to reach services on the other side, and the proxy in between should be able to control who goes where without reading the traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The initiator sends nested tunnel elements that form a source route. Each proxy strips the outermost element and connects onward. When the last hop answers ok, every proxy simply copies octets between its two connections.
tldr.outcome: The end machines can then negotiate TLS between themselves. RFC 3620 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8553.

today: RFC 3620 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8553. It has not been obsoleted. The text itself says nothing about deployments.

sections.title: Rationale: A Tunnel Built from BEEP Peers
sections.content:
The TUNNEL profile lets cooperating BEEP peers form an application-layer tunnel. The peers exchange tunnel elements that specify a source route. The outermost element is stripped off and used to decide the next hop. The innermost, empty tunnel element tells the final destination that it is the final destination. Any BEEP peer other than the initiator and the final destination is called a proxy.

In one use, a BEEP peer implementing the profile sits with a firewall. A machine inside the firewall connects to the proxy and asks it to connect to an endpoint outside. Once connected, the proxy tells the outside endpoint that it will be tunneling. If that machine agrees, the proxy gets out of the way and passes octets transparently, and both ends perform a tuning reset, much as starting TLS discards cached session state.

Another use is to limit connections to outside servers by user identity negotiated through SASL. The RFC also notes the profile can anonymize the true source of a BEEP connection, much as a NAT does, but leaves detailed discussion of that out.
sections.eli5: You tell a helper at the gate who you want to reach. The helper opens a line to them, then steps aside and just passes notes back and forth without reading them.

sections.title: Examples: One Hop, Two Hops and Failures
sections.content:
In the one-hop example, initial connects to proxy1 and sees its greeting, then starts a TUNNEL channel carrying <tunnel fqdn='final.example.com' port='604'> wrapping an empty <tunnel/>. Proxy1 connects to final, starts a TUNNEL channel carrying just the empty element, and relays the ok it receives. Immediately after sending ok, proxy1 passes octets transparently until either transport connection closes, then closes the other. The next greeting may include the TLS profile, so the end machines can talk without the proxy interfering undetected.

In the two-hop example the initiator nests a second tunnel element for the final machine inside the first, and each proxy peels one layer. If the destination is not a BEEP server, or does not support the TUNNEL profile, the attempt fails and an error goes back along the chain. The RFC's failing case is a telnet service that answers with login:.

A non-BEEP destination can be accepted on purpose: the initiator leaves out the innermost empty element, the last proxy does not expect a BEEP greeting, and afterwards the initiator exchanges raw, non-BEEP data with the final machine.

The profile and endpoint attributes route without naming every hop. A proxy locally configured to know where a profile such as SEP2 or an endpoint such as operator console lives maps it to a fuller route. The RFC says endpoint routes to a particular server, while profile routes to a particular service.
sections.eli5: Each helper on the path opens one door, then steps aside. If the last door leads somewhere that does not speak the right language, the news that it failed is passed back down the line.

sections.title: The tunnel Element
sections.content:
The only element defined is tunnel, which may contain at most one nested tunnel. Its optional attributes are fqdn, ip4, ip6, port, srv, profile and endpoint. Formats: fqdn is a fully qualified domain name, ip4 is a dotted quad, ip6 follows RFC 2373, port is a decimal number from one to 65535, srv is a pair of underscore-prefixed identifiers such as _sep._tcp, profile is a URI, and endpoint is any string allowed as an attribute value.

Only these attribute combinations are allowed: fqdn + port; fqdn + srv; fqdn + srv + port; ip4 + port; ip6 + port; and, only on the innermost element, profile, endpoint, or no attributes at all.
sections.eli5: The message is like nested boxes. Each box says where to go next, and the smallest box is empty and means you have arrived.

sections.title: What Each Peer Does with a Tunnel Request
sections.content:
When a TUNNEL channel starts, the listener examines the outermost tunnel element. With no attributes, this peer hosts the BEEP service the initiator wants, so it performs a tuning reset: all channels including channel zero are implicitly closed, cached session information is discarded, and a new plaintext greeting is sent.

With fqdn and port but no srv, the name is looked up as an A record in DNS. ip4 and ip6 give addresses directly. With srv, the srv value and fqdn are joined with a period and looked up as an SRV record; if that fails and port is present, the connection is tried as though srv were absent. A profile or endpoint element must have no nested elements, and the proxy decides the route, giving hop-by-hop routing rather than source routing.

If the outermost element has no nested element but has other attributes, this peer is the final BEEP hop. An ok is returned as soon as the final transport connection is up, and no BEEP greeting from the far side is expected. If the server cannot be contacted, an error is returned. If the contacted server offers no BEEP greeting or no TUNNEL profile when a nested element exists, that is also an error.

Otherwise the peer is a proxy: it strips the outer element, starts a new TUNNEL channel on the outgoing session and sends the inner element. An error in reply is passed back unchanged after closing the outgoing session. An ok is passed back, and starting with the octet after the closing trailer of the final frame of the reply carrying ok, the proxy copies octets between the two connections without interpretation.

If a transport security layer such as TLS has already been negotiated, the TUNNEL semantics are ill-defined, and the profile MUST NOT be advertised in any greeting after transport security has been negotiated.
sections.eli5: Each helper reads the top box. Empty box: it is the end of the line. Box with an address: open a line there and hand over the smaller box inside. Once the line is open, the helper only passes things along without reading them.

sections.title: Reply Codes
sections.content:
The profile defines eleven three-digit error codes, from 421 (service not available, for example when the proxy lacks resources) to 554 (transaction failed, for example a policy violation). Several concern authentication and authorization: 530, 534 and 537. Code 538 means encryption is already enabled.

The RFC distinguishes two similar failures. 450 fits when the destination machine could not be contacted. 550 fits when it could be contacted but the next phase of the protocol could not be negotiated. It is suggested that the start of any reply from the destination be included in the CDATA of the error element for debugging.
sections.eli5: Each kind of failure has a number, so the helper can say exactly what went wrong: nobody home, wrong language, or you are not on the guest list.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
TUNNEL is a BEEP profile, and in BEEP transport security, user authentication and data exchange are orthogonal. Because the profile deliberately allows contact between two machines normally separated by a firewall, it should be configured with care. It is reasonable to strictly limit the hosts and services a proxy may contact, and to limit use to authorized users identified through a SASL profile.

Negotiating TLS end to end after the tunnel is established stops intermediate proxies from observing or modifying the cleartext, but only if certificates are properly configured. A proxy could mount a man-in-the-middle attack if public key infrastructure is not deployed.

Where exposing internal machine names across a firewall is undesirable, source routing can reach the firewall proxy, with an innermost profile or endpoint that only the firewall proxy understands. Per the RFC this prevents sniffers from seeing addresses on the other side, and prevents attackers from probing many names through source routing and reading the error messages. For the second protection, the proxy must allow only profile or endpoint connections. Requiring SASL identification before a TUNNEL channel starts also thwarts the probing, at higher overhead.
sections.eli5: A gatekeeper should only let the right people through and only to the right places. If friends then lock their messages with their own key, even the gatekeeper cannot read them.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the profile with the URI http://iana.org/beep/TUNNEL. The channel-creation message and one-to-one exchange start are tunnel, positive replies use ok and negative replies use error. Any extensions MUST be documented in a Standards Track RFC.

A single well-known TCP port, 604, is allocated to the TUNNEL profile, with short name tunnel. The SRV identifier _tunnel is also reserved, so the srv attribute _tunnel._tcp MAY be used as a default for finding the tunnel entry point of a domain.
sections.eli5: The profile got its own name tag and its own door number, 604, in the official lists.
